title: Sherlock Holmes and Silver Blaze
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
retoldBy: Retold for Grammar Stream from “Silver Blaze” by Arthur Conan Doyle (1892)
blurb: Cases for Young Detectives. The fastest racehorse in England vanishes a week before the big race, and his trainer is found hurt on the moor. Can Sherlock Holmes find Silver Blaze in time, and what does the dog that did nothing in the night-time have to do with it?
note: A retelling for young readers. In Doyle’s story the trainer, John Straker, is killed by the horse’s kick; here he is knocked out and wakes at the end to confess. Who did what, and every clue Holmes uses (the curry, the silent dog, the surgeon’s knife, the bill, the lame sheep, the hoofprints), are unchanged. Opium becomes “a sleeping powder”; Straker’s secret life is kept vague; the police theory about travellers camping on the moor and the original race card are left out. “Clue check” questions are added.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Missing Champion
paragraphs: “I am afraid, Watson, that I shall have to go,” said Holmes one morning at breakfast. “To Dartmoor.”

I was not surprised. All England was talking about the case. Silver Blaze, the finest racehorse in the country, had vanished from his stable only a week before the great race for the Wessex Cup. And his trainer, John Straker, had been found lying out on the moor, badly hurt.
An hour later we were speeding west in a railway carriage. Holmes glanced out of the window and then at his watch.
“We are going well,” he said. “Fifty-three and a half miles an hour.”
“How can you possibly know that?”

“The telegraph posts beside this railway are sixty yards apart. I count how many we pass in a minute. The sum is an easy one.” He leaned forward. “Now, let me tell you the facts. Nothing makes a problem clearer than explaining it to somebody else.

“Silver Blaze has never lost a race. He is the favourite for the Wessex Cup next Tuesday, and enormous sums of money have been bet on him. So there are many people who would be very glad if he did not run.

“He lives at King’s Pyland, a small stable on the lonely moor. His trainer, John Straker, used to be a jockey and has always seemed an honest man. Every night, one stable lad sleeps in the stable to guard the horses, with a big dog, while the other two lads sleep in the loft upstairs. Two miles away, across the moor, is another stable called Mapleton. Its trainer, Silas Brown, has a horse called Desborough, the second favourite for the Cup.

“Last Monday night, a lad called Ned Hunter was on guard. The maid, Edith, carried his supper down from the house. It was curried mutton, a spicy meat dish. She took nothing to drink, because there was a water tap in the stable.

“On the dark path, a stranger stepped into the light of her lantern. He was a pale, nervous gentleman in a grey tweed suit, carrying a heavy stick. He held out a folded piece of white paper. ‘See that the boy has this tonight,’ he said, ‘and you shall have the prettiest dress that money can buy.’

“Edith was frightened and ran on to the little window where she always handed in the supper. But the stranger followed and leaned in. ‘Tell me about the horses for the Wessex Cup,’ he said to the lad, ‘and you won’t be sorry.’
“Ned Hunter was furious. He ran across the stable to let the dog loose, and Edith fled back to the house. But when Hunter rushed out with the dog, the stranger had gone.”
“One moment,” I said. “When the lad ran out, did he leave the stable door unlocked?”
“Excellent, Watson, excellent!” said Holmes. “I sent a telegram to ask that very question. No. He locked the door behind him. And the window is too small for a man to climb through.”
Clue check: What do you think was on that folded piece of paper? Keep an eye on the curry, and on the dog!

chapters.title: Chapter 2. A Morning on the Moor
paragraphs: “At one o’clock in the morning,” Holmes went on, “Mrs Straker woke and found her husband getting dressed. He said he was worried about the horses and was going down to check on them. It was pouring with rain. She begged him to stay, but he pulled on his big raincoat and went out.

“At seven o’clock, he had still not come back. Mrs Straker hurried down to the stable with the maid. The door was wide open. Ned Hunter was slumped in a chair, so deeply asleep that nobody could wake him. Silver Blaze’s stall was empty.

“They searched the moor. A quarter of a mile away, they found Straker’s raincoat hanging on a gorse bush. Just beyond it was a muddy hollow, and at the bottom lay John Straker, knocked out cold by a blow to the head. He is still in a deep sleep, and the doctor says it may be days before he wakes. In one hand he held a small, very sharp knife. In the other he clutched a red and black silk scarf, which the maid knew at once. The stranger had been wearing it.

“The mud showed that Silver Blaze had been in that hollow too. But since that morning, nobody has seen him. And when Hunter’s supper was tested, it had a strong sleeping powder mixed into it. Yet the people at the house ate the very same curry that night, and slept perfectly normally.”
“And the police?”

“Inspector Gregory has arrested the stranger. His name is Fitzroy Simpson. He bets on horse races, and he has bet a great deal of money that Silver Blaze will *not* win. He admits he came to find out about the horses, but says he meant no harm. His clothes were wet from the storm. His stick is heavy enough to have struck the blow. And his scarf was in the trainer’s hand. The police think Simpson drugged the lad, opened the stable with a spare key and led the horse away, and that Straker caught him and they fought.” Holmes shook his head. “But where is the key? And where could a stranger hide the most famous horse in England?”

It was evening when we reached Tavistock, in the middle of the great round moor. Colonel Ross, the owner of Silver Blaze, a small, neat, sharp-eyed gentleman, was waiting for us with Inspector Gregory, a tall man with a lion-like beard. We drove out across the moor, where the ferns were bronze in the fading light, and stopped beside the trainer’s red-brick house. We all climbed out, except Holmes. He sat staring at the sky, lost in thought, until I touched his arm.
“Excuse me,” he said to the Colonel. “I was daydreaming.”
But I knew him well. There was a gleam in his eye that told me he had seen a clue.
Clue check: The sleeping powder was hidden in a spicy curry. Could Fitzroy Simpson have known that the lad would be eating curry that night? Who *could* have known?

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Clues in a Tin Box
paragraphs: Inside, the Inspector opened a tin box and laid out what had been in Straker’s pockets: a box of matches, two inches of candle, a pipe, a silver watch, five gold coins, some papers, and a small ivory-handled knife with a very thin blade.
“This is a strange knife,” said Holmes. “Watson, this is surely in your line?”
“It is a surgeon’s knife,” I said, “for very delicate operations.”
“A strange thing to carry on a rough, rainy night. It would not even fold up to fit in a pocket. And the papers?”
“Bills for hay, a letter from the Colonel, and a bill from a dressmaker in London, made out to a Mr William Derbyshire,” said the Inspector. “Mrs Straker says he was a friend of her husband’s.”
Holmes glanced at the bill. “Thirty-seven pounds! Mr Derbyshire has expensive tastes. Twenty-two guineas is a great deal for a single dress.”
As we left the room, a pale, worried woman stepped forward. It was Mrs Straker.
“Surely I met you at a garden party in Plymouth, Mrs Straker?” said Holmes. “You wore a dress of dove-grey silk, trimmed with ostrich feathers.”
“I never had such a dress, sir,” she said.
“Ah, that quite settles it,” said Holmes, and with an apology he followed the Inspector outside.
A short walk brought us to the muddy hollow. At its edge was the gorse bush.
“There was no wind that night, I understand?” said Holmes.
“None, but very heavy rain.”
“Then the coat was not blown on to the bush. Somebody took it off and put it there.”

Holmes lay down flat on a piece of matting, with his chin in his hands, and studied the trampled mud. “Hullo!” he said. “What’s this?” He held up a half-burnt match, so coated in mud that it looked like a chip of wood.
“I can’t think how I missed it,” said the Inspector crossly.
“It was buried in the mud. I only saw it because I was looking for it.”
“You *expected* to find it?”
“I thought it likely.”
Holmes took a horseshoe that had belonged to Silver Blaze and put it in his pocket. “For luck,” he said.
“Should we take my horse out of the race, Mr Holmes?” asked the Colonel impatiently.
“Certainly not. Let his name stand.”
The Colonel and the Inspector went back to the house. Holmes and I walked out across the moor, as the sun sank behind the stables of Mapleton.
Clue check: Why might somebody take off his coat on a cold, rainy night? And why would he need a match and a candle out on the moor?

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Hoofprints in the Mud
paragraphs: “Let us leave aside, for now, the question of who struck down John Straker,” said Holmes, “and think about the horse. A horse likes company. If Silver Blaze ran away, he would go home to King’s Pyland or across to Mapleton. If he were wandering on the open moor, somebody would have seen him by now. He is not at King’s Pyland. So he must be at Mapleton.
“The ground here is hard and dry. But over there is a long hollow that must have been very wet on Monday night. If I am right, that is where we shall find his tracks.”

Holmes went to the left of the hollow and I went to the right. I had not taken fifty steps when I heard him shout. There in the soft earth was the print of a hoof. Holmes took the horseshoe from his pocket. It fitted exactly.
“See the value of imagination, Watson,” he said. “We imagined what might have happened, acted on it, and found we were right. Come on!”
We followed the tracks, losing them and finding them again, until we were close to Mapleton. Then Holmes pointed. Beside the hoofprints was a new set of tracks: a man’s.
“The horse was alone before!” I cried.
“Exactly. Now a man is leading him.”
The tracks turned back towards King’s Pyland. But I happened to glance aside and saw the same tracks coming back again, the other way.
“One for you, Watson!” said Holmes. “You have saved us a long walk.”
The return tracks led straight to the gates of Mapleton. A fierce old man came striding out with a riding whip.
“Be off, or I’ll set the dog on you!” he shouted.
Holmes leaned forward and whispered something in his ear. The man went bright red. “It’s a lie!”
“Very well. Shall we argue about it out here, or in your parlour?”
“Oh, come in if you must.”
Twenty minutes later Holmes came out again, and I have never seen a man so changed as Silas Brown. His face was pale, his hands shook, and his bullying had vanished.
“It shall all be done, sir,” he stammered. “It shall be there. Should I change it back first, or not?”
Holmes thought, then burst out laughing. “No, don’t. I shall write to you.”

As we walked away, he explained. “Silas Brown has the horse, Watson. His boots have the same square toes as the footprints we followed. I told him exactly what he had done, so he thinks I was watching him. Early on Tuesday morning, he saw a strange horse wandering on the moor. When he saw the white blaze on its forehead, he knew it was Silver Blaze, the only horse that could beat his own in the race! He began to lead it home to King’s Pyland. Then a wicked idea came to him. He turned round, led it back to Mapleton, and hid it.”
“Will the horse be safe with him?”
“He will guard it like treasure. His only hope is to bring it back safe and sound. And, Watson, say nothing to the Colonel. He has been rather rude to me, and I mean to have a little fun with him.”
“And what about John Straker?”
“Oh, we are going back to London on the night train.”
I was thunderstruck. How could he give up now?

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Dog in the Night-Time
paragraphs: “My friend and I are going back to London tonight,” Holmes told the Colonel and the Inspector. “But I have every hope that your horse will run on Tuesday. Please have your jockey ready. And Inspector, may I borrow a photograph of Mr Straker?”
“I must say I am disappointed in your famous friend,” the Colonel muttered to me. “We are no further on than when he came.”
As we climbed into the carriage, Holmes leaned out and spoke to a stable lad.
“You have some sheep in the field. Have you noticed anything wrong with them lately?”
“Nothing much, sir. But three of them have gone a bit lame.”
Holmes chuckled and rubbed his hands. “A long shot, Watson, a very long shot!” he said. “Inspector, let me recommend to your attention this curious illness among the sheep.”
The Colonel still looked unimpressed, but the Inspector was watching Holmes closely.
“Is there anything else you want me to notice?” he asked.
“The curious incident of the dog in the night-time.”
“But the dog did nothing in the night-time.”
“That was the curious incident,” said Sherlock Holmes.

Clue check: When the stranger came, the dog was ready to chase him. But later that night, somebody came in and led a horse out, and the dog did not bark at all, not even enough to wake the lads asleep upstairs. What does that tell you about the person who came in?

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Wessex Cup
paragraphs: Four days later, we were at the racecourse at Winchester. Colonel Ross looked very cold and cross.
“I have seen nothing of my horse,” he said.
“I suppose you would know him if you saw him?” said Holmes.
“A child would know Silver Blaze,” snapped the Colonel, “with his white forehead and his speckled front leg!”
Six horses came out. A powerful brown horse cantered past us, and its jockey wore the Colonel’s colours: a black cap and a red jacket.
“That’s not my horse!” cried the Colonel. “That beast hasn’t a single white hair on his body! What have you done, Mr Holmes?”
“Well, well, let us see how he gets on,” said Holmes calmly, looking through my binoculars. “An excellent start! Here they come!”

What a race it was! The six horses thundered up the straight so close together that you could have covered them all with one carpet. Halfway up, the yellow cap of Desborough pushed into the lead, and the crowd roared. But then the Colonel’s horse came with a tremendous rush, swept past Desborough, and flashed past the winning post a good six lengths ahead!
“Well, it’s my race,” gasped the Colonel, “but I can’t make head or tail of it.”

“Come and look at the horse,” said Holmes. “Wash his face and his leg with a little spirit, and you will find he is the same old Silver Blaze as ever. Somebody had dyed his white patches, and I let him run just as he was.”
“My dear sir, you have done wonders! Forgive me for doubting you. Now, if only you could find the person who struck down poor John Straker.”
“I have done so,” said Holmes quietly. “He is standing right behind you.”
The Colonel went red with anger. But Holmes only laughed, stepped past him, and laid his hand on the glossy neck of the horse.
“The horse!” cried the Colonel and I together.
“Yes, the horse. And it may help him if I say he did it in self-defence, and that John Straker did not deserve your trust at all.”
On the train home, Holmes explained.

“My first clue was the curry. I realised it in the carriage, when I seemed to be daydreaming. Sleeping powder has a taste, but a spicy curry would hide it perfectly. Simpson could not possibly have chosen what the Strakers cooked that night. So only the Strakers could have planned it. And since the others ate the same curry without falling asleep, the powder was added after the lad’s dish was set aside.
“Then there was the dog. Somebody led a horse out of the stable in the night, and the dog did not bark. So it was somebody the dog knew very well.

“I was almost sure that John Straker himself took Silver Blaze out on to the moor. But why? That tiny surgeon’s knife told me. It could make a very small, secret cut on a horse’s leg. The horse would go a little lame and lose the race, and everybody would think he had simply strained it. Straker had bet money *against* his own horse. He could not do it in the stable, because the horse would kick and wake the lads. So he led him to the hollow, where nobody could see his light.”
“The villain!” cried the Colonel. “So that is why he had the candle and the matches.”

“Exactly. He took off his coat to do his delicate work, and struck a match. But the horse was frightened by the sudden light, and seemed to sense that something bad was going to happen. He lashed out, and his iron shoe struck Straker on the head. And Simpson’s scarf? Simpson dropped it as he ran away, and Straker picked it up, perhaps meaning to tie the horse’s leg with it.
“As for the sheep, I guessed that such a careful man would practise his trick first. And so he had.

“Last of all, the bill. Men do not carry other men’s bills in their pockets. I was sure ‘Mr William Derbyshire’ was Straker himself, living a secret, grand life under another name and spending far more money than he had. That was why he needed to win his bets. Mrs Straker had never seen that expensive dress. And when I took Straker’s photograph to the dressmaker in London, she knew him at once as her best customer, Mr Derbyshire.”
“Wonderful!” cried the Colonel. “But where was the horse?”
“He ran away, and one of your neighbours looked after him,” said Holmes. “I think we must forgive that neighbour, now that the horse is safely home.”

When John Straker woke up at last, he told the whole sorry truth, just as Holmes had said. Fitzroy Simpson was set free. And Silver Blaze, once his face had been washed, was the most famous racehorse in England.
